Many years ago, I wrote an essay for a psychology class in college. It was a glimpse into the bipolar-II mixed hypomanic-depressive episode. The prof asserted that everything a person does seems logical to them, no matter how twisted the logic may seem from the outside. In one page, I blew her away and completely changed her mind. Following is the unabridged text:

---

**The Tenth Circle**

Bipolar disorder has three central features: mania, depression, and so-called mixed states. These mixed states are acute episodes during which mania and depression mix. It is hard to imagine how this mixing plays out a priori, so I'll paint a picture.

First, you have to imagine mania. Your thoughts rush. You could be thinking several trains of thought at once or switching between a number of them very rapidly, keeping each going at (at least) a normal pace. You have incredible amounts of energy; anything is possible. Your synapses are flooded with dopamine, so you feel incredible. Your muscles are stronger, your brain faster, and life is beautiful.

But then something happens. A single bad thought makes its way into the churning mix. It passes in an instant, processed in the blink of an eye and expelled as the poison it is just as quickly. But the taint remains. Soon other thoughts turn darker. They multiply rapidly, replacing the good thoughts. Soon all of your thoughts have turned dark, but it doesn't stop there. Your thoughts turn darker and darker, the mania multiplying the depression and the depression coloring everything around it. To a first order approximation, your thoughts get darker faster the more depressed you become. This, by the way, describes exponential growth, a concept whose significance in this context should speak for itself.

Soon you enter a circle of hell even Dante himself couldn't have fathomed, one unimaginable to anyone who hasn't been there. Your thoughts turn on you, each other, and themselves. Rational thought disintegrates; at least a third of your thoughts lack any trace of logic. You engage in self-destructive behaviors, some rational and some irrational. Many people turn to drugs or commit suicide. These are rational: they stop the episode, and it must be stopped at any cost. But what if you can't bring yourself to stop the episode and want nothing more than for it to continue? This is the point at which rational actions simply go out the window.

You do things that you know will only make matters worse and exacerbate the suffering; you can't help yourself. One particularly dangerous aspect is interaction with other people. You tell the wrong people your most destructive secrets, exaggerated secrets, things spun in the worst possible direction and put into the worst light, and even things made up totally, all in the name of self- destruction.

There is no reason here. No catharsis or relief comes as a result. You can't see any reason, no matter how twisted, for your actions. This is a state of mind without logic.
